decks.title: Orientation
decks.summary: What Vim is, and what this course is for.

cards.title: What Vim is
body: Vim is a *modal* editor. In Normal mode the letter keys are commands rather than characters: `d` deletes, `w` moves forward a word, `u` undoes. You type text only once a command has asked for it.
Bram Moolenaar released Vim in 1991 as **Vi IMproved**, extending Bill Joy's `vi` from 1976. It has been maintained by its community since Moolenaar died in 2023.
The keys are a grammar, not a list of shortcuts. An operator takes a range, so `d` plus `w` is `dw`. Once you know the parts, combinations you have never typed still work.
notes: Commands are written here the way Vim's own manual writes them: `Ctrl-v` means the Control key held with `v`.

cards.title: Why this course exists
body: The goal is not typing faster. It is making a predictable edit **once** and then replaying it — with `.`, a count, a macro, or `:g` — instead of performing it by hand fifty times.
So the grammar comes first and the automation layer second: motions and operators, then text objects, registers, ranges, substitution, macros, and `:global`.

Terminal Vim is the baseline throughout, because those same keys are what an editor's Vim mode reproduces. Nothing here needs a `.vimrc` — this course does not teach configuration, plugins, or Vimscript.
notes: A few chords are claimed by default in some editors. Every one of them works in Vim; the *Chords an editor may claim* card lists which to check.

cards.title: Where to start
body: The lessons never open or close a file — every exercise begins with a buffer already on screen. So the commands that *do* open and close files, `:w`, `:q`, `ZZ`, live on cards of their own rather than in a lesson that would contradict itself.
Read those six cards now, or never. They stay one tap away under **☰ Contents → Reference**, along with the chords an editor may claim.

decks.title: Standalone Vim survival
decks.summary: Opening, writing, leaving, and reaching the shell — the commands an exercise cannot honestly teach.

cards.title: Leaving safely
cards.lede: A buffer is *modified* when it holds changes you have not written. Vim refuses to abandon one unless you insist.

rows.vim: Write the buffer to its file. The file changes; Vim stays open.
rows.host: Works. In VS Code's Vim mode it saves exactly as `Cmd`/`Ctrl-S` would — and the editor may be saving on its own schedule as well.

rows.vim: Close the window. Refused while the buffer is modified.
rows.host: Closes an editor tab rather than a Vim window. In VS Code that is the whole editor, not one split.

rows.vim: Write, then close. `:x` writes only when something changed; `:wq` touches the file either way.
rows.host: Both land on save-and-close-tab. The `:x` distinction — write only when something changed — usually disappears.

rows.vim: The Normal-mode form of `:x`. No colon, no Enter.
rows.host: Normally available: it is a Normal-mode key, so the Vim mode handles it without the host being asked.

rows.vim: **Quit and discard.** Every unwritten change in that buffer is gone.
rows.host: Closes the tab without saving. VS Code will often still restore the text from its own local history, so *discarded* is less final than in a terminal.

rows.vim: Act on every open window at once. `:qa!` discards all of them.
rows.host: Usually acts on the whole window — more than you meant if you only wanted one file gone.

notes: The forced forms — `:q!`, `ZQ`, `:qa!` — are the only ones that throw work away. The rest refuse rather than destroy.
`:w {file}` writes somewhere else and leaves you editing the original.

cards.title: Files and buffers
cards.lede: A *buffer* is text in memory. A *window* is a viewport onto a buffer. A *tab page* is a layout of windows. Closing a window does not discard its buffer.

rows.vim: Open a file into a buffer, creating it if it does not exist.
rows.host: VS Code's quick open (`Cmd`/`Ctrl-P`) is the usual route, and `:e` often works alongside it.

rows.vim: Reload the current file from disk, discarding unwritten changes.
rows.host: Maps onto revert-file where the host offers one.

rows.vim: List the buffers Vim holds, with their numbers and flags.
rows.host: Usually missing. VS Code tracks open editors itself, and its tab strip is the nearest equivalent.

rows.vim: Point this window at another buffer. A partial name is enough when it is unambiguous.
rows.host: Replaced by quick open. Buffer numbers do not exist in the host's model.

rows.vim: Unload a buffer. Refused while it is modified.
rows.host: Closes an editor tab. VS Code has no separate notion of a loaded but hidden buffer.

rows.vim: Jump to the alternate buffer — the fastest way back to the file you just left.
rows.host: Usually unbound. VS Code's go-back walks locations rather than files, so it is close but not the same.

notes: The `:ls` flags worth reading: `%` current, `#` alternate, `+` modified, `h` loaded but hidden.
A modified buffer can be hidden rather than written. That is why `:q` complains about files you thought you had closed.

cards.title: Windows
cards.lede: Splits show two places at once: two files, or two parts of the same file.

rows.vim: Split horizontally. With no file name, both windows show the same buffer.
rows.host: Splits the editor group.

rows.vim: Split vertically.
rows.host: Splits the editor group side by side, as VS Code's own `Cmd`/`Ctrl-\` does.

rows.vim: Move focus left, down, up, right between windows.
rows.host: Check this one first: VS Code binds `Ctrl-w` to close-editor by default, so the whole window-motion prefix is the first thing you lose.

rows.vim: Close the focused window. The buffer stays loaded.
rows.host: Closes the editor tab, dropping the view and the file together — not the same as closing a Vim window.

rows.vim: Close every window except this one.
rows.host: Usually unbound; the host has its own close-others.

rows.vim: Even out the window sizes.
rows.host: Usually unbound.

notes: Splits do not duplicate text. Two windows on one buffer edit the same lines, and both update as you type.
`:sp {file}` and `:vs {file}` open and split in one step.

cards.title: Help
cards.lede: Vim's manual is a set of buffers, navigated with the motions this course teaches.

rows.vim: Open the manual at its front page, in a split.
rows.host: Missing. VS Code ships its own documentation instead.

rows.vim: Jump to a topic. Prefixes select the mode: `:help i_CTRL-R` is Insert, `:help v_o` is Visual, `:help :w` is an Ex command.
rows.host: Missing.

rows.vim: Follow the tag under the cursor.
rows.host: Usually bound elsewhere. VS Code's go-to-definition covers the code case but not the manual.

rows.vim: Pop back up the tag stack, undoing the last `Ctrl-]`.
rows.host: Usually unbound.

rows.vim: Search the whole manual, then walk the hits with `:cn` and `:cp`.
rows.host: Missing.

notes: Help opens in a split, so `:q` closes the help and leaves your file untouched.
Prefixes let one key have several entries: `:help CTRL-R` and `:help i_CTRL-R` describe different commands.

cards.title: Starting Vim with work queued
cards.lede: Vim is also a batch text processor. These forms run commands before — or instead of — showing you an editor, which is where this course's automation stops being interactive.
cards.hostNote: These are shell invocations, not editor commands. They run in any terminal — VS Code's integrated terminal included — and an editor's Vim mode plays no part in them.

rows.vim: Open a file for editing.
Open the file, then run an Ex command. Repeat `-c` for more: `vim -c '%s/old/new/g' -c 'wq' notes.txt` edits and exits.
Ex mode, silent: no screen, no interaction. This is how you script Vim's editing from a shell.
The same idea spelled with `ex`: run the command, then `x` writes and exits.
Open read-only, so a stray keystroke cannot change the file.

notes: Quote the command, or the shell will eat `%`, `*`, and `!` before Vim sees them.
This is where `:%s`, `:g`, and `:normal` stop being something you type and start being something you schedule.

cards.title: Filters and the shell
cards.lede: `!` hands lines to an external program and puts its output back. It is Vim's escape hatch to everything the shell can do.

rows.vim: Replace every line with the output of `sort`.
rows.host: Works where a real Vim runs underneath — vscode-neovim, or VSCodeVim with its Neovim integration enabled. A pure reimplementation has no shell to hand the lines to.

rows.vim: Filter only the lines a Visual selection covers.
rows.host: Same split: real Vim underneath yes, a reimplementation no.

rows.vim: The Normal-mode form. `!ap sort` filters the paragraph the cursor sits in.
rows.host: Same.

rows.vim: Read a command's output in below the cursor: `:r !date`.
rows.host: Same.

rows.vim: Send the buffer to a command's input without changing it: `:w !wc -l`.
rows.host: Same.

notes: Watch where the `!` sits: `:r !cmd` reads output *in*, `:w !cmd` writes the buffer *out*. The buffer only changes in the first case.
A filter that fails can leave the range mangled. `u` puts it back.

decks.title: Chords an editor may claim
decks.summary: Keys this course teaches that an embedding editor commonly binds to something else.

cards.title: Chords an editor may claim
cards.lede: **Every one of these works in terminal Vim.** The right column is what an embedding editor commonly takes for itself — the defaults below are VS Code's, and other hosts differ in the details rather than in the problem. This is why a practiced key sometimes does nothing at all.

rows.vim: Page forward.
rows.host: Find.

rows.vim: Page back.
rows.host: Toggle sidebar.

rows.vim: Scroll down one row, cursor held.
rows.host: Quick open.

rows.vim: Scroll up one row, cursor held.
rows.host: Redo.

rows.vim: Half a page down.
rows.host: Add a cursor at the next match.

rows.vim: Jump back through the jump list.
rows.host: Usually free in VS Code; occasionally taken.

rows.vim: Delete the word before the cursor, in Insert mode.
rows.host: Close editor.

rows.vim: Redo in Normal mode; insert a register in Insert mode.
rows.host: Recent files.

rows.vim: Visual Block.
rows.host: Paste, on Windows and Linux.

rows.vim: Increment or decrement the number under the cursor.
rows.host: Select all; cut.

notes: `gq` and `=` reformat and re-indent using `textwidth` and `equalprg`. Both need those set — in terminal Vim as much as anywhere else.
`:normal` and `:global` support in an embedded Vim emulator is usually narrower than the real thing. Where a host runs a real Vim underneath, they behave.
None of this is a reason to stop using a command. It is a reason not to be confused when one does nothing.

decks.title: Worth knowing, not drilled
decks.summary: Useful occasionally, easy to look up — once you know they exist.

cards.title: Worth knowing, not drilled
cards.lede: These earn a mention rather than a lesson.

rows.vim: Open the command-line *window*: your Ex or search history as an editable buffer. Edit a past line with ordinary motions and press Enter to run it.
rows.host: Missing in a reimplementation; present where a real Vim runs underneath.

rows.vim: Move through the undo *tree* by state or by time. `:earlier 10m` is the buffer as it stood ten minutes ago; plain `u` only ever walks one branch.
rows.host: Missing. VS Code keeps one linear undo history, plus a separate timeline of saved versions.

rows.vim: The selection registers. On X11 `"*` is the primary selection and `"+` the clipboard; on Windows and macOS they are the same thing. `"+y` yanks to the system clipboard.
rows.host: Wired to the real system clipboard in VS Code and most hosts. **In this course `"+` is an internal register** — Vim Wilds never touches your device clipboard.

rows.vim: Case conversion inside a `:s` replacement. `\u` and `\l` change one character; `\U` and `\L` run until `\E`. So `:s/\w\+/\u&/g` capitalises every word.
rows.host: Runs where a real Vim does the substitution. VSCodeVim's own `:s` does not implement them.

rows.vim: Evaluate an expression as the replacement: `:s/\d\+/\=submatch(0)+1/` adds one to every number.
rows.host: Real Vim only.

notes: Case conversion and `\=` are described here rather than practised: this course's editor does not run them, so drilling them would teach a keystroke it could not check.
